extracted.intended_audience: federal agency lawyers, rulewriters, OMB/OIRA staff, DOJ counsel, and policymakers involved in administrative rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended standards for when and how federal agencies may invoke the APA 'good cause' exemption to forgo pre-promulgation notice-and-comment and for selecting and managing NCFRs, DFRs, and IFRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticable standard for invoking good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency can claim notice-and-comment is 'impracticable' when 'due and timely execution of its functions would be impeded by the notice otherwise required in [§ 553].' (Attorney General’s Manual) Examples include safety investigations requiring immediate rules and short-term activities for which agencies receive limited advance notice (e.g., Coast Guard security/safety zones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must show that providing notice-and-comment would impede timely execution; courts require concrete threats to health/environment or an emergency rather than mere 'technical' amendments (Utility Solid Waste Activities Group v. EPA). Use narrow, fact-specific justifications (e.g., imminent safety/national security/health threats). Provide clear explanation in the Federal Register notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnecessary standard for invoking good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA’s reference to 'unnecessary' refers to issuance of a minor rule 'in which the public is not particularly interested' — routine determinations, insignificant in nature and impact, inconsequential to industry/public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate where a rule is purely procedural, formulaic, administrative, and involves no exercise of discretion (examples: OPM's SSN procedural DFR; NMFS ACE allocations based on formulaic fishing histories). Agencies should issue NCFRs or DFRs in such cases and explain why prior rulemaking or statutory prescription makes comment unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrary to the public interest standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'public interest' ground applies when requiring advance notice would defeat the public interest (e.g., enable the financial manipulation the rule seeks to prevent). Emergency situations (national security, public health crises) often justify this ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with caution and specific factual support. Examples where courts upheld this ground include vaccine mandates for healthcare workers during COVID (public health emergency) and suspending airman certificates for security threats (national security). Agencies commonly combine 'public interest' with 'impracticable' or 'unnecessary' claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to fairly determine and adequately explain basis for good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should invoke good cause only after they have 'fairly determined, and adequately explained in a Federal Register notice,' that notice-and-comment is impracticable, unnecessary, and/or contrary to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble must present factual and legal justification. Courts scrutinize these explanations and construe the exemption narrowly and reluctantly; insufficient explanation risks judicial invalidation (e.g., Utility Solid Waste Activities Group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of instrument: NCFR, DFR, or IFR
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must decide whether to implement a rule under a Notice of a Noncontroversial Final Rule (NCFR), Direct Final Rule (DFR), or Interim Final Rule (IFR) when invoking good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA offers little guidance on choosing among these instruments; agencies should explain choice in notice. For DFRs, agencies should anticipate and plan for adverse comments and have companion proposed rules when appropriate. For IFRs, agencies must still finalize after comment and should set expectations for finalization timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-promulgation comment opportunity (ACUS/ABA recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies promulgate rules under the good cause exemption because notice-and-comment is 'impracticable' or 'contrary to the public interest,' they should invite interested persons to submit post-promulgation comments and set a target date to adopt a successor rule after considering comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ABA recommended specifics: (i) invite public comments post-promulgation; (ii) set a target date for adopting a successor rule; (a) if agency misses target, explain and set a new date; (b) adequacy of compliance not subject to judicial review but existing remedies for undue delay remain; (c) the preamble and record for the successor rule should support the lawfulness of the rule as a whole (not just differences). ACUS and GAO have similar recommendations. Agencies should implement these practices to increase public participation and timely finalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and timely finalization of IFRs
rubrics_metrics.description: IFRs take effect immediately but by their terms must later be promulgated as final rules after considering comments; agencies often delay finalization, which undermines public engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include allowing IFRs to expire if agencies fail to finalize by a date certain, OIRA pressing agencies to finalize, and considering self-imposed or mandated limits on how long an IFR can remain in effect before finalization. Agencies should aim for expeditious completion and provide explanations if delays occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review and gatekeeper role
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA (within OMB) reviews proposed regulations and DFRs/IFRs for significant rules and serves as a gatekeeper, with the ability to approve, withhold approval, and press agencies to finalize IFRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA tends to review DFRs quickly but can keep IFR files open and encourage finalization. OIRA-issued guidance could be used to encourage agencies to respond to comments on final major rules issued without prior notice. Agencies should expect OIRA scrutiny, and OIRA can withhold approval of rules that fail to meet guidance standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department of Justice guidance principles
rubrics_metrics.description: DOJ guidance documents should recognize that they do not bind the public or have the force of law, should be labeled as guidance, and should cite the source of any binding legal requirements being described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Garland Memorandum's principles: label guidance as guidance; cite legal sources; recognize guidance is nonbinding. DOJ could issue government-wide guidance on the good cause exemption (possibly via a notice-and-comment process) and could condition its defense of agencies on compliance with such guidance to give it weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduce incorporated-by-reference standards when access is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rule incorporates private standards by reference that are behind paywalls, agencies should consider reproducing the standards in full in the final rule to avoid access and constitutional issues (Milice v. CPSC problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leaving binding regulatory content inaccessible to the public; reproduction in the final rule or ensuring public access prevents procedural and constitutional challenges and avoids premature judicial challenges based on promulgation date ambiguities.

rubrics_metrics.name: DFR finalization notice and treatment of adverse comments
rubrics_metrics.description: A DFR that receives no adverse comments becomes final on the date specified in the original Federal Register notice; agencies should issue a second FR notice indicating the DFR has taken effect, though this is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If significant adverse comments are received, agencies should quickly withdraw the DFR and reissue it as a proposed rule with opportunity for comment or proceed with a companion proposed rule (which will be subject to full OIRA review). Agencies should avoid leaving the public uncertain about a DFR's finality (Milice illustrates unfairness when promulgation date triggers statutory challenge periods before rule finality is known).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair timing for judicial challenges (promulgation date clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized problems when the date used to determine the statute-of-limitations for challenging a rule (e.g., date of DFR publication) precedes the agency's final decision to make the rule final after comments are addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should provide clarity on when a rule is 'promulgated' for purposes of judicial review—e.g., by ensuring DFR finalization and issuing follow-up notices—so parties are not forced to file premature suits before knowing whether a rule will become final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple good-cause rationales together
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies often rely on more than one good-cause ground (public interest, impracticable, unnecessary) in combination when forgoing notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining grounds can be appropriate, but agencies should provide independent factual justification for each ground relied upon and explain how they interrelate. Courts will evaluate the sufficiency of each asserted ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance stakeholder consultation where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when pre-promulgation notice-and-comment is impracticable, agencies should afford better advance consultation with affected stakeholders where feasible (CRA example: agencies should have engaged stakeholders before issuing a last-minute IFR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive consultation can reduce post-promulgation controversy and improve rule quality. Agencies should document outreach efforts in the Federal Register notice to demonstrate good faith and reduce claims of dilatory or arbitrary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts’ approach: narrow construction and reluctance to countenance exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have cautioned that the good cause exemption be 'narrowly construed and reluctantly countenanced.' Agencies must convince courts they are not engaging in dilatory tactics and must justify temporary measures installed without public airing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should avoid using good cause to evade notice-and-comment for major rules; provide strong factual record and timetables, and minimize the period of interim measures. Judicial precedents (e.g., Mid-Tex, Mack Trucks, Utility Solid Waste) show courts will scrutinize claims and require agencies to demonstrate need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligation to respond to post-promulgation comments and finalize rules transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency issues an IFR or similar instrument without prior notice-and-comment, it is still obligated to consider public comments and finalize the rule with a full explanation of the basis for the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should respond to significant comments, finalize promptly, and ensure the preamble and administrative record support the lawfulness of the successor rule as a whole. Failure to do so undermines public participation and may invite recommendations (ACUS/GAO/ABA) or judicial criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential reforms and forms of guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Four paths for providing better guidance on use of the good cause exemption: (1) amend the APA; (2) Presidential Executive Order; (3) Department of Justice guidance; (4) OIRA guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider tradeoffs: statutory amendment offers enforcement certainty but less flexibility and political feasibility; Executive Orders are durable but reversible and less enforceable for independent agencies; DOJ guidance carries persuasive weight and could condition defense of agencies; OIRA guidance leverages gatekeeper role but raises concerns about delay and review. Choose form consistent with desired enforceability and flexibility.
